title: Describe a pattern rule in words and numbers (start at …, add … each time)

lesson.title: Start At, Add Each Time

steps.say: You already know how to keep a pattern going, like four, seven, ten, and then thirteen. Today we learn how to say the rule out loud, so anyone can build the pattern without seeing your paper.

visual.caption: Sofia's savings jar, week by week

steps.say: A pattern rule always has two little pieces. Piece one is where you start. Piece two is what you do every single time to get the next number. That is it, just those two pieces.

Let's find both pieces in Sofia's savings jar. She starts with four dollars in week one, so the start is four. Now look at the jumps. Four to seven is a jump of three. Seven to ten is a jump of three. Ten to thirteen is a jump of three. The same jump every time, so the rule is: start at four, add three each time.

visual.caption: Same jump of 3 dollars from week to week

steps.say: Here is a mix-up lots of kids make. Someone looks at four, seven, ten, thirteen and says the rule is add four, because the pattern starts at four. But four is the starting number, not the jump. The jump is what you add to get from one number to the next, and that is three. If you added four each time, you would get four, eight, twelve, sixteen, which is a different pattern altogether.

visual.caption: Adding 4 makes a whole different pattern

steps.say: So when you describe a pattern, tell people both pieces: where to start, and what to add each time. Two pieces, and the whole pattern is theirs.

lesson.answer: A pattern rule needs two pieces: start at ___, and add ___ each time.

practice.question: Liam is growing a sunflower on his balcony in Victoria. He measures it every week and writes down: 6 centimetres, 11 centimetres, 16 centimetres, 21 centimetres. Describe the pattern rule in words and numbers: start at what, and add what each time?
practice.answer: Start at 6 centimetres, add 5 centimetres each time. (Because 11 minus 6 is 5, 16 minus 11 is 5, and 21 minus 16 is 5.)
